content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/MissingBulbWebsite/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the repo's scheduled `conversation-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

Comment class: feature (a content-strategy rethink — I'm giving you the proposal first; I'll implement once you pick a direction, since promoting research findings onto the site is your call under the product-wiki wall).

I went back over the research in `product-wiki/` (brand, audience, consulting-market) — it has real, cited findings that never made it into requirements, and they point at concrete display decisions. Here's my rethink.

## What the current page gets wrong

The current site is a flat list: four equal service cards, nine equal project cards. That makes the visitor do the sorting, and it leans on the portfolio for proof it can't deliver — every repo is 0-stars and created mid-2026, so a visitor who clicks through gets activity, not adoption. The research is blunt about this: ~48% of B2B buyers weight peer recommendation above all other content, and ~69% notice website-vs-reality contradictions and walk. The GitHub links *are* the consistency test, so the site must claim exactly what the repos show — no more.

## What to promote instead

**1. Lead with the thing that's actually differentiated: Claudinite + the practice it proves.** "AI Software Management" is a coinage — no established category uses it — which is fine *only if the site defines it*. One sentence, anchored by the working system: *managing software development where AI agents do the engineering, governed by shared guidelines and automated checks*. Claudinite isn't one project among nine; it's the evidence the category is real. The strongest, most honest boast available is dogfooding: **this website itself is built, checked, and maintained by AI agents under Claudinite, and the repo is public** — every PR, every automated check, inspectable. That's proof no competitor page has, and it's verifiable in one click.

**2. Curate the portfolio; stop listing it.** Reframe from "projects we're proud of" (a claim of significance the star-counts contradict) to "working code you can read" (a claim of transparency the repos confirm). Show 3–4 with a *what-this-demonstrates* line — e.g. GoogleCalendarEventCreator (shipping a real Chrome extension), TLDR (a community web product), EdFringeNow (a fast, focused site) — and collapse the rest into one "everything else we build is public too → org link". LaughCounter, gRatio, VascularColoring as equal cards dilute rather than add.

**3. Promote *how we work* — currently absent, and it's the section that sells.** 67% of B2B buyers now prefer buying without talking to a rep; for a firm with no sales team the site substantially *is* the sales conversation, so it has to qualify and reassure on its own. A "How an engagement runs" section — small team, hands-on building not decks, working software in weeks, scoped/capped engagements — matches exactly the axis where boutiques are documented to beat the big firms (cost, speed, hands-on). The category norm is "contact us" with no numbers; publishing even a starting price or engagement shape would be a genuine differentiator, but that's your call.

**4. Be direct about newness rather than silent.** The org is weeks old and the repo dates say so. A short, plain "who we are" line that states real experience directly (whatever predates the org) beats letting visitors infer the firm's age from the portfolio. This is the section I can't write without you — I won't invent credentials.

**5. A real contact path.** Right now "Work with us" ends at a GitHub link. A commercial site needs an actual channel (an email, a form). Also unfilled without your input.

## What *not* to add

Market-size numbers, testimonials we don't have, breadth claims (the portfolio is 13/15 JavaScript — web and extensions, so claim craft in that lane, not "full-stack everything"), and any case-study section until there's a real engagement to put in it.

I'd restructure the page as: **hero (define AI Software Management) → the Claudinite proof / self-maintaining-site story → how an engagement runs → curated code showcase → who we are → contact.** Wording stays plain throughout — the promotion is in what's given space, not in adjectives.

> ⚠️ **Still open — your decisions before I implement:**
> 1. Approve the restructure above (any section to drop/add)?
> 2. Who-we-are: what real pre-2026 experience/credentials may the site state?
> 3. Contact channel: publish an email (which?), a form, or GitHub-only for now?
> 4. Pricing/engagement shape: publish a starting number or engagement model, or stay "get in touch"?
> 5. Which 3–4 projects headline the showcase (my pick: Claudinite, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, TLDR, EdFringeNow)?
>
> Answer any subset and I'll build it; I'll also record the approved points as requirements in `product-wiki/product-requirements/` so the wall is crossed properly.

It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc. - **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of. - **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. # The task lifecycle The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill. For every new task: 1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work. 2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`). 3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done. --- # HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. --- # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape, growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc (`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`). - **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. - **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header. - **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header doesn't move. - **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may build on. - **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current. - **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open questions in both directions. - **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR. - **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones. - **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline. --- # tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md), [single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md), [single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)). The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.** - **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites **its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body. --- # session-tooling — rules ## Never use WebFetch to obtain content you must have `WebFetch` fails two different ways in this environment, and both were paid for in one session: - **It summarizes.** Asked for "the complete verbatim content" of a raw `githubusercontent.com` file, it returned a prose description of the document instead. The file had to be re-fetched with `curl -sSL -o /f.md ` and read from disk — the correct move the first time. - **It 403s.** Four consecutive fetches of ordinary publisher pages (`gartner.com`, `fortunebusinessinsights.com`, `marketdataforecast.com`, `squarerootseo.com`) all returned `403 Forbidden`, so a research pass ended up attributing figures to search snippets instead of verifying them at source. So: when the content itself matters, `curl` it into the scratchpad and `Read` it. When a page 403s, do **not** retry it or try a sibling URL — take the `WebSearch` snippet, attribute it to the publisher rather than asserting it, and flag it for re-verification. `WebSearch` itself works fine and is the right first reach. **`codeload.github.com` is blocked here too** — `curl … | tar -xz` of a repo tarball returns 403. Use `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com//`, which works through the proxy and yields the same tree. ## A ToolSearch that finds nothing does not mean the tool is absent Deferred tools are matched by keyword, and the keywords are not the tool's own vocabulary. Promoted by the owner in session on 2026-07-30 (issue #15), distilled from the
[brand](../brand/README.md), [audience](../audience/README.md) and

   Missing Bulb's coinage; the site's hero must define it in one plain

   dogfooding: Missing Bulb runs its own software development with AI agents
   under Claudinite (public on GitHub). Promote that over any breadth claim.

   GoogleCalendarEventCreator, TLDR and EdFringeNow with a
   what-this-demonstrates line each; collapse the rest to the org link. Frame
   the section as "working code you can read" (transparency), not adoption or
   significance the 0-star repos cannot support.
4. **Sell the engagement, not adjectives.** A "how an engagement runs" section:
   small team, hands-on building, working software in weeks, scoped
   engagements. No published pricing — the call to action is "get in touch".

   founder Ariel Raunstien with facts from his public profile (roles at Google
   and Google for Startups Israel, and Paidy; a CS degree), linking his
   LinkedIn. No invented credentials; the site's claims must match what a
   visitor finds when they check.
6. **A real contact channel:** contact@missingbulb.com.
7. **Exclusions.** No market-size figures, no testimonials or case studies
   until a real one exists, no breadth-of-engineering claims beyond what the
   portfolio (web and browser-extension work) shows.

Missing Bulb
  • The practice
  • How we work
  • Code
  • Who we are
  • Contact

AI Software Management

Running software development where AI agents do the engineering — governed by shared guidelines and automated checks, so the work stays fast and trustworthy. That is Missing Bulb's specialty. Around it, we do software, management, and AI consulting.

See it working Get in touch

Not a pitch — a working practice

We don't advise on AI-assisted development from the sidelines. We run our own projects this way, every day.

Claudinite — the system

Our open-source corpus of working guidelines, skills, and automated conformance checks for AI coding agents. It decides how an agent names things, structures commits, ties work to issues, and what a change must pass before it lands. Every rule is public — you can read exactly how we keep agent-written software honest.

Dogfooded daily

Missing Bulb's own repositories — this website among them — are built and maintained by AI agents working under Claudinite's rules, with automated checks gating every merge.

What we bring to you

The same practice, applied to your team: where agents fit in your development lifecycle, the guardrails that keep their output reviewable, and the process changes that make the speed real.

How an engagement runs

Small and hands-on

You work directly with the people doing the work. No layers, no handoffs, no slide decks standing in for software.

Working software in weeks

Engagements are scoped to deliver something running early — a working system you can react to, not a long discovery phase.

Scoped, not open-ended

We agree on the outcome and the boundaries up front. When the scope is done, the engagement is done.

Get in touch

Working code you can read

Our public work is on GitHub — not as a trophy shelf, but so you can read the code and judge the craft before you ever talk to us. A few that show the range:

  • Claudinite

    Guidelines, skills, and automated checks for AI coding agents. Shows: the AI Software Management practice itself, as running code.

  • Google Calendar Event Creator

    A Chrome extension that turns any webpage describing an event into a Google Calendar event. Shows: shipping real browser-extension product work.

  • TLDR

    Community-generated tl;dr descriptions for any link on the web. Shows: building a community web product end to end.

  • EdFringeNow

    A website to help you find an Edinburgh Fringe show. Shows: a focused, useful site shipped fast.

Everything else we build is public too — browse the rest in the missingbulb GitHub organization.

Who we are

Missing Bulb is run by Ariel Raunstien, a software engineer and consultant. Before founding Missing Bulb, Ariel worked at Google and with Google for Startups Israel, and at Paidy; he holds a BA in Computer Science from the Open University of Israel. Missing Bulb itself is new — the working practice behind it is not.

Get in touch

Tell us what you're building and where AI fits — or where you'd like it to. We'll reply with how we'd approach it.

contact@missingbulb.com We're on GitHub

© 2026 Missing Bulb · contact@missingbulb.com · GitHub

Missing Bulb is a software consultancy. We do software, management, and AI consulting — including AI Software Management consulting: helping teams run software development where AI agents do real engineering work.

What we do

Software consulting

Design, build, and ship. We write working software — web apps, browser extensions, and the tooling around them — and everything we make is public, so you can read the code before you talk to us.

Management consulting

How software teams plan, decide, and deliver. We help you shape the process around the code: what to build, in what order, and how to know it's working.

AI consulting

Practical AI in real products and real workflows — from putting a model behind a feature to putting AI agents to work inside your development process.

AI Software Management consulting

Our specialty: managing software development done with AI. We don't just advise on it — we run our own projects this way, and we built Claudinite, our open system of shared working guidelines and automated checks that keeps coding agents productive and honest.

Projects we're proud of

All of our work lives in the open, in the missingbulb GitHub organization. A few highlights:

  • Claudinite

    A shared corpus of working guidelines, skills, and automated checks for AI coding agents — the system behind our AI Software Management practice. This very website is built and maintained under it.

    Community-generated tl;dr descriptions for any link on the web.

  • LaughCounter

    A thing that listens and counts the laughs.

  • gRatio

    A small JavaScript project — the code speaks for itself.

Work with us

The fastest way to see how we work is to read our code. Then come say hello.

input.body:
## What changed

Owner-approved content rethink of the website (decided in session; the five decisions are recorded in issue #15):

**`site/index.html`** — restructured from a flat services-plus-nine-projects list to:

1. **Hero defines "AI Software Management"** in one sentence — it's our coinage, so the site defines it rather than assuming it lands.
2. **"Not a pitch — a working practice"** — leads with Claudinite (public, inspectable) and the dogfooding claim: our own repos are built by AI agents under its rules, checks gating every merge.
3. **"How an engagement runs"** — small and hands-on, working software in weeks, scoped engagements; CTA is "Get in touch" (no published pricing).
4. **Curated showcase** — Claudinite, Google Calendar Event Creator, TLDR, EdFringeNow, each with a *Shows:* line naming what it demonstrates; the rest collapse to the org link. Framed as "working code you can read", not a trophy shelf.
5. **Who we are** — states the founder's background directly from his public profile (Google, Google for Startups Israel, Paidy; CS degree), linking LinkedIn, and is explicit that the firm is new.
6. **Contact** — contact@missingbulb.com in the contact section and footer.

**`site/styles.css`** — small additions for the *Shows:* lines and section CTA.

**`product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md`** — the approved decisions are recorded as requirements 1–7 (including the exclusions: no market figures, no invented credentials, no breadth claims), so the wiki wall is crossed by the human-reviewed sink as the standard requires.

## Notes

- Claims were kept to what a visitor can verify: Claudinite is public; this repo is private, so the dogfooding wording avoids claiming this site's repo is inspectable.
- Claudinite world sweep passes; page verified rendering in headless Chromium.

Closes #15

AI Software Management

Running software development where AI agents do the engineering — governed by shared guidelines and automated checks, so the work stays fast and trustworthy. That is Missing Bulb's specialty. Around it, we do software, management, and AI consulting.

See it working Get in touch

Not a pitch — a working practice

We don't advise on AI-assisted development from the sidelines. We run our own projects this way, every day.

Claudinite — the system

Our open-source corpus of working guidelines, skills, and automated conformance checks for AI coding agents. It decides how an agent names things, structures commits, ties work to issues, and what a change must pass before it lands. Every rule is public — you can read exactly how we keep agent-written software honest.

Dogfooded daily

Missing Bulb's own repositories — this website among them — are built and maintained by AI agents working under Claudinite's rules, with automated checks gating every merge.

What we bring to you

The same practice, applied to your team: where agents fit in your development lifecycle, the guardrails that keep their output reviewable, and the process changes that make the speed real.

How an engagement runs

Small and hands-on

You work directly with the people doing the work. No layers, no handoffs, no slide decks standing in for software.

Working software in weeks

Engagements are scoped to deliver something running early — a working system you can react to, not a long discovery phase.

Scoped, not open-ended

We agree on the outcome and the boundaries up front. When the scope is done, the engagement is done.

Get in touch

Working code you can read

Our public work is on GitHub — not as a trophy shelf, but so you can read the code and judge the craft before you ever talk to us. A few that show the range:

  • Claudinite

    Guidelines, skills, and automated checks for AI coding agents. Shows: the AI Software Management practice itself, as running code.

  • Google Calendar Event Creator

    A Chrome extension that turns any webpage describing an event into a Google Calendar event. Shows: shipping real browser-extension product work.

  • TLDR

    Community-generated tl;dr descriptions for any link on the web. Shows: building a community web product end to end.

  • EdFringeNow

    A website to help you find an Edinburgh Fringe show. Shows: a focused, useful site shipped fast.

Everything else we build is public too — browse the rest in the missingbulb GitHub organization.

Who we are

Missing Bulb is run by Ariel Raunstien, a software engineer and consultant. Before founding Missing Bulb, Ariel worked at Google and with Google for Startups Israel, and at Paidy; he holds a BA in Computer Science from the Open University of Israel. Missing Bulb itself is new — the working practice behind it is not.

Get in touch

Tell us what you're building and where AI fits — or where you'd like it to. We'll reply with how we'd approach it.

contact@missingbulb.com We're on GitHub

© 2026 Missing Bulb · contact@missingbulb.com · GitHub

# Product requirements — Missing Bulb website

The human-reviewed sink. Research from the wikis in this tree arrives here only
by a human's hand; no unattended pass edits this folder. This is the only
`product-wiki/` content the website's own code and content may build on.

The owner's stated intent below gives the growth passes their frame; the
Requirements section holds the findings the owner has since promoted.

## Stated intent (owner, at adoption)

- **The product** — a static commercial website for Missing Bulb. It boasts
  about Missing Bulb's projects, all of which live in GitHub. Missing Bulb also
  does software, management, and AI consulting, including AI Software Management
  consulting.
- **The audience** — people interested in the services of a software consultancy
  firm, in AI, and in the software development life cycle; plus people
  interested in the projects Missing Bulb builds. Deliberately wide, and the
  research is expected to stay scoped rather than survey the whole field.
- **The category** — software, management and AI consulting, including AI
  Software Management consulting. The competitor set is not yet named.

## Requirements

Promoted by the owner in session on 2026-07-30 (issue #15), distilled from the
[brand](../brand/README.md), [audience](../audience/README.md) and
[consulting-market](../consulting-market/README.md) findings:

1. **Define the category, don't assume it.** "AI Software Management" is
   Missing Bulb's coinage; the site's hero must define it in one plain
   sentence, anchored by Claudinite as the working example.
2. **Lead with Claudinite as proof of practice.** The strongest honest claim is
   dogfooding: Missing Bulb runs its own software development with AI agents
   under Claudinite (public on GitHub). Promote that over any breadth claim.
3. **Curate the portfolio rather than list it.** Feature Claudinite,
   GoogleCalendarEventCreator, TLDR and EdFringeNow with a
   what-this-demonstrates line each; collapse the rest to the org link. Frame
   the section as "working code you can read" (transparency), not adoption or
   significance the 0-star repos cannot support.
4. **Sell the engagement, not adjectives.** A "how an engagement runs" section:
   small team, hands-on building, working software in weeks, scoped
   engagements. No published pricing — the call to action is "get in touch".
5. **State experience directly; never imply it.** A who-we-are section names
   founder Ariel Raunstien with facts from his public profile (roles at Google
   and Google for Startups Israel, and Paidy; a CS degree), linking his
   LinkedIn. No invented credentials; the site's claims must match what a
   visitor finds when they check.
6. **A real contact channel:** contact@missingbulb.com.
7. **Exclusions.** No market-size figures, no testimonials or case studies
   until a real one exists, no breadth-of-engineering claims beyond what the
   portfolio (web and browser-extension work) shows.

1	// Cloudflare Web Analytics — privacy-first, cookieless visitor counts.
2	//
3	// Cloudflare Web Analytics sets no cookies, stores no personal data, and can't
4	// track visitors across sites, so it needs no consent banner (see privacy.html).
5	//
6	// The beacon token is NOT a secret — it ships in the client and is visible to
7	// every visitor — so it lives in a GitHub Actions *variable* (not a secret):
8	//   repo Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions -> Variables ->
9	//   CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN
10	// The Pages deploy (.github/workflows/pages.yml) injects that value into the
11	// placeholder below at build time, the same way js/build-info.js is stamped.
12	//
13	// TO ENABLE: create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics ->
14	// "Add a site"), then add its token as the CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN repo variable.
15	// It works on GitHub Pages as-is — no hosting or DNS move to Cloudflare needed.
16	//
17	// Until a real token is injected (variable unset, or running locally), this
18	// loader does nothing: no beacon is requested, so the site keeps its "no
19	// analytics" behaviour and never ships a broken tag.
20	(function () {
21	  var TOKEN = 'REPLACE_WITH_CLOUDFLARE_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN';
22	  // Bail out while the placeholder is still in place (startsWith, ES5-safe).
23	  if (!TOKEN || TOKEN.lastIndexOf('REPLACE_WITH', 0) === 0) return;
24	
25	  var beacon = document.createElement('script');
26	  beacon.defer = true;
27	  beacon.src = 'https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js';
28	  beacon.setAttribute('data-cf-beacon', JSON.stringify({ token: TOKEN }));
29	  (document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(beacon);
30	})();

# Publishes site/ to GitHub Pages on every push to main that touches it.
# Artifact-flow deploy (no gh-pages branch); the custom domain (claudinite.com)
# is configured in the repository's Pages settings, not here — see
# site/README.md. Uploading site/ (never the repo root) keeps the agent-tooling
# dirs out of the artifact.
name: Deploy site to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - 'site/**'
      - '.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml'
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
        with:
          # First run enables Pages (source: GitHub Actions) if the token is
          # allowed to; otherwise enable it once in Settings → Pages.
          enablement: true
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: site
      - id: deployment

# site/ — claudinite.com

The static marketing site for Claudinite. No build step, no dependencies: the
directory is published as-is by [.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml](../.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml)
(GitHub Pages via the actions artifact flow) on every push to `main` that
touches `site/**`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is | Who edits it |
|---|---|---|
| [index.html](index.html) | The one page: evergreen copy + the four mechanism explainers | Rarely — structure and evergreen claims |
| [assets/style.css](assets/style.css) | The whole design system (tokens at the top) | Rarely |
| [assets/main.js](assets/main.js) | Animations + rendering of the promoted-content slots | Rarely |
| [data/promoted.js](data/promoted.js) | **The promoted content: stats, spotlight, pack cards, updates** | **Every promo refresh — edit this, usually nothing else** |

## Updating promoted content (the expected frequent, agentic change)

`data/promoted.js` is the single file a routine promo run edits. Contract:

- **Truthful and verifiable.** Every stat, count, and update must be checkable
  against the vendored canon packs in this repo or against its history. No
  aspirational numbers, no invented dates.
- **`updates`** — newest first, ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` dates, ≤ 140 chars, only
  shipped facts. Keep at most 6 entries; drop the oldest.
- **`spotlight`** — the 3–5 features currently being promoted, ordered; the
  first entry renders full-width (visual priority). Taglines ≤ 90 chars.
- **`packs`** — one card per canon pack. When a pack lands in or leaves the
  canon, mirror it here and refresh `stats`.
- **`canonRef`** — keep in step with the `ref` stamp in
  [../.claudinite-checks.json](../.claudinite-checks.json) (short form).
- Keep the file a plain script (`window.CLAUDINITE = {...}`) — it must run
  from `file://` with no module loader.

Evergreen sections (hero, mechanisms, adopt, FAQ) state how Claudinite works;
change them only when the product's mechanisms actually change.

## Local preview

Open `index.html` directly, or `python3 -m http.server -d site` and browse
`http://localhost:8000`.

## Custom domain

The Pages artifact flow takes its domain from the repository's Pages settings
(no `CNAME` file needed). When claudinite.com is connected there, the
`<link rel="canonical">` in `index.html` is already correct.
===CI===
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - name: Claudinite world-scope conformance sweep
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs

content.content:
EdFringeNow ← Back

Privacy

Last updated 2 July 2026

The short version: no cookies, no tracking, no personal data — just an anonymous count of how many people visit.

EdFringeNow is a static website. It runs entirely in your browser. There are no accounts, no sign-up, and no server of ours behind it — so there is nothing about you for us to receive, log, or keep.

We don't sell your data, and we don't track you across the web. No ads. No advertising trackers. No cookies set by us. The one thing we do measure is anonymous, aggregate visitor numbers — see Analytics below.

Analytics

To understand roughly how many people use EdFringeNow, we use Cloudflare Web Analytics — a privacy-first tool chosen precisely because it doesn't use cookies, doesn't store personal data, and can't identify you or follow you to other sites. It records anonymous, aggregate signals only: page views, the referring site, and a broad region worked out from your request (your IP address is used to derive that, but is never stored). No cross-site tracking, no advertising profile — which is also why there's no cookie-consent banner to click through.

Your location

If you allow location access, your position is used only in your browser to work out which shows are near you. It is never sent to us or to anyone else. Deny it and the app simply falls back to central Edinburgh — everything still works.

What your browser loads

Like any web page, opening EdFringeNow fetches a few files from other services. Those services see your IP address and browser as part of a normal web request, the same as visiting any website:

  • Map tiles from OpenStreetMap.
  • The map library (unpkg) and typefaces (Google Fonts) from their content delivery networks.
  • The privacy-first analytics beacon (a small script) from Cloudflare.

The show and venue listings are plain files served from this site. They describe the festival, not you.

Links out

“Open in Maps” opens Google Maps, and ticket links open edfringe.com. Once you follow a link, that site's own privacy policy applies — not this one.

Questions

Email support@edfringenow.com.

© 2026 Missing Bulb

@@ -0,0 +1,30 @@
+// Cloudflare Web Analytics — privacy-first, cookieless visitor counts.
+//
+// Cloudflare Web Analytics sets no cookies, stores no personal data, and can't
+// track visitors across sites, so it needs no consent banner (see privacy.html).
+//
+// The beacon token is NOT a secret — it ships in the client and is visible to
+// every visitor — so it lives in a GitHub Actions *variable* (not a secret):
+//   repo Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions -> Variables ->
+//   CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN
+// The Pages deploy (.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml) injects that value into
+// the placeholder below at build time.
+//
+// TO ENABLE: create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics ->
+// "Add a site"), then add its token as the CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN repo variable.
+// It works on GitHub Pages as-is — no hosting or DNS move to Cloudflare needed.
+//
+// Until a real token is injected (variable unset, or running locally), this
+// loader does nothing: no beacon is requested, so the site keeps its "no
+// analytics" behaviour and never ships a broken tag.
+(function () {
+  var TOKEN = 'REPLACE_WITH_CLOUDFLARE_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN';
+  // Bail out while the placeholder is still in place (startsWith, ES5-safe).
+  if (!TOKEN || TOKEN.lastIndexOf('REPLACE_WITH', 0) === 0) return;
+
+  var beacon = document.createElement('script');
+  beacon.defer = true;
+  beacon.src = 'https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js';
+  beacon.setAttribute('data-cf-beacon', JSON.stringify({ token: TOKEN }));
+  (document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(beacon);
+})();

AI Software Management

Running software development where AI agents do the engineering — governed by shared guidelines and automated checks, so the work stays fast and trustworthy. That is Missing Bulb's specialty. Around it, we do software, management, and AI consulting.

See it working Get in touch

Not a pitch — a working practice

We don't advise on AI-assisted development from the sidelines. We run our own projects this way, every day.

Claudinite — the system

Our open-source corpus of working guidelines, skills, and automated conformance checks for AI coding agents. It decides how an agent names things, structures commits, ties work to issues, and what a change must pass before it lands. Every rule is public — you can read exactly how we keep agent-written software honest.

Dogfooded daily

Missing Bulb's own repositories — this website among them — are built and maintained by AI agents working under Claudinite's rules, with automated checks gating every merge.

What we bring to you

The same practice, applied to your team: where agents fit in your development lifecycle, the guardrails that keep their output reviewable, and the process changes that make the speed real.

How an engagement runs

Small and hands-on

You work directly with the people doing the work. No layers, no handoffs, no slide decks standing in for software.

Working software in weeks

Engagements are scoped to deliver something running early — a working system you can react to, not a long discovery phase.

Scoped, not open-ended

We agree on the outcome and the boundaries up front. When the scope is done, the engagement is done.

Get in touch

Working code you can read

Our public work is on GitHub — not as a trophy shelf, but so you can read the code and judge the craft before you ever talk to us. A few that show the range:

  • TLDR

    Community-generated tl;dr descriptions for any link on the web. Shows: building a community web product end to end.

  • EdFringeNow

    A website to help you find an Edinburgh Fringe show. Shows: a focused, useful site shipped fast.

Everything else we build is public too — browse the rest in the missingbulb GitHub organization.

Who we are

Missing Bulb is run by Ariel Raunstien, a software engineer and consultant with a career spanning engineering and startup work — his profile has the detail. Missing Bulb itself is new; the working practice behind it is not.

input.body:
## What this adds

Cookieless Cloudflare Web Analytics, following the pattern EdFringeNow already runs in production.

- **`site/analytics.js`** — a loader holding a placeholder token. While the placeholder is in place (locally, or when the variable is unset) it returns immediately: no beacon is requested, so the site keeps its no-analytics behaviour and never ships a broken tag.
- **`.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml`** — a build-time step substituting the token from the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repo **variable**. The beacon token is public (it ships in the client and is visible to every visitor), so it belongs in a variable, not a secret. `sed` uses `#` as its delimiter so the line contains no shell pipe.
- **`site/privacy.html`** + a footer link — the disclosure ships in the same commit as the behaviour it describes.
- **`site/styles.css`** — a few rules for the legal page layout.

## Verification

Both states exercised in headless Chromium against the real files, using the identical `sed` line the workflow runs:

| State | Beacon requests | `data-cf-beacon` |
|---|---|---|
| Placeholder (unset variable) | 0 | absent |
| Token injected | 1 | `{"token":"deadbeefcafe1234"}` |

Claudinite world sweep passes.

## To turn it on

Create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics → "Add a site"), then add its token as the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repo variable (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables). It works on GitHub Pages as-is — no hosting or DNS move needed. Until then the site deploys exactly as it does today, with analytics off.

Closes #19

+// Cloudflare Web Analytics — privacy-first, cookieless visitor counts.
+//
+// Cloudflare Web Analytics sets no cookies, stores no personal data, and can't
+// track visitors across sites, so it needs no consent banner (see privacy.html).
+//
+// The beacon token is NOT a secret — it ships in the client and is visible to
+// every visitor — so it lives in a GitHub Actions *variable* (not a secret):
+//   repo Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions -> Variables ->
+//   CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN
+// The Pages deploy (.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml) injects that value into
+// the placeholder below at build time.
+//
+// TO ENABLE: create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics ->
+// "Add a site"), then add its token as the CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN repo variable.
+// It works on GitHub Pages as-is — no hosting or DNS move to Cloudflare needed.
+//
+// Until a real token is injected (variable unset, or running locally), this
+// loader does nothing: no beacon is requested, so the site keeps its "no
+// analytics" behaviour and never ships a broken tag.
+(function () {
+  var TOKEN = 'REPLACE_WITH_CLOUDFLARE_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN';
+  // Bail out while the placeholder is still in place (startsWith, ES5-safe).
+  if (!TOKEN || TOKEN.lastIndexOf('REPLACE_WITH', 0) === 0) return;
+
+  var beacon = document.createElement('script');
+  beacon.defer = true;
+  beacon.src = 'https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js';
+  beacon.setAttribute('data-cf-beacon', JSON.stringify({ token: TOKEN }));
+  (document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(beacon);
+})();

Privacy

The short version: no cookies, no tracking, no personal data — just an anonymous count of how many people visit.

claudinite.com is a static website. It runs entirely in your browser. There are no accounts, no sign-up, and no server of ours behind it — so there is nothing about you for us to receive, log, or keep.

We don't sell your data, and we don't track you across the web. No ads, no advertising trackers, no cookies set by us. The one thing we measure is anonymous, aggregate visitor numbers.

Analytics

To understand roughly how many people visit, we use Cloudflare Web Analytics — a privacy-first tool chosen precisely because it doesn't use cookies, doesn't store personal data, and can't identify you or follow you to other sites. It records anonymous, aggregate signals only: page views, the referring site, and a broad region worked out from your request (your IP address is used to derive that, but is never stored). No cross-site tracking and no advertising profile — which is also why there's no cookie-consent banner to click through.

What your browser loads

This site ships no webfonts, no frameworks, and no third-party assets beyond one thing: the privacy-first analytics beacon (a small script) from Cloudflare. That service sees your IP address and browser as part of a normal web request, the same as visiting any website.

Links out

Links to GitHub open that site. Once you follow a link, that site's own privacy policy applies — not this one.

Questions

Open an issue on the canon repository.

# site/ — claudinite.com

The static marketing site for Claudinite. No build step, no dependencies: the
directory is published as-is by [.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml](../.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml)
(GitHub Pages via the actions artifact flow) on every push to `main` that
touches `site/**`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is | Who edits it |
|---|---|---|
| [index.html](index.html) | The one page: evergreen copy + the four mechanism explainers | Rarely — structure and evergreen claims |
| [assets/style.css](assets/style.css) | The whole design system (tokens at the top) | Rarely |
| [assets/main.js](assets/main.js) | Animations + rendering of the promoted-content slots | Rarely |
| [data/promoted.js](data/promoted.js) | **The promoted content: stats, spotlight, pack cards, updates** | **Every promo refresh — edit this, usually nothing else** |

## Updating promoted content (the expected frequent, agentic change)

`data/promoted.js` is the single file a routine promo run edits. Contract:

- **Truthful and verifiable.** Every stat, count, and update must be checkable
  against the vendored canon packs in this repo or against its history. No
  aspirational numbers, no invented dates.
- **`updates`** — newest first, ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` dates, ≤ 140 chars, only
  shipped facts. Keep at most 6 entries; drop the oldest.
- **`spotlight`** — the 3–5 features currently being promoted, ordered; the
  first entry renders full-width (visual priority). Taglines ≤ 90 chars.
- **`packs`** — one card per canon pack. When a pack lands in or leaves the
  canon, mirror it here and refresh `stats`.
- **`canonRef`** — keep in step with the `ref` stamp in
  [../.claudinite-checks.json](../.claudinite-checks.json) (short form).
- Keep the file a plain script (`window.CLAUDINITE = {...}`) — it must run
  from `file://` with no module loader.

Evergreen sections (hero, mechanisms, adopt, FAQ) state how Claudinite works;
change them only when the product's mechanisms actually change.

## Local preview

Open `index.html` directly, or `python3 -m http.server -d site` and browse
`http://localhost:8000`.

## Custom domain

The Pages artifact flow takes its domain from the repository's Pages settings
(no `CNAME` file needed). When claudinite.com is connected there, the
`<link rel="canonical">` in `index.html` is already correct.

input.body:
## What this adds

Cookieless Cloudflare Web Analytics, following the pattern EdFringeNow already runs in production.

- **`site/assets/analytics.js`** — a loader holding a placeholder token. While the placeholder is in place (locally, on `file://`, or when the variable is unset) it returns immediately: no beacon is requested, so the site keeps its no-analytics behaviour and never ships a broken tag. No external assets are added to the default build, so the site's "no webfonts, no frameworks, no third-party assets" property holds until the token is deliberately set.
- **`.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml`** — a build-time step substituting the token from the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repo **variable**. The beacon token is public (it ships in the client and is visible to every visitor), so it belongs in a variable, not a secret. `sed` uses `#` as its delimiter so the line contains no shell pipe.
- **`site/privacy.html`** + nav and footer links — the disclosure ships in the same commit as the behaviour it describes, styled with the existing design tokens.
- **`site/README.md`** — the layout table gains rows for both new files, so the documented layout doesn't drift.

## Verification

Both states exercised in headless Chromium against the real files, using the identical `sed` line the workflow runs:

| State | Beacon requests | `data-cf-beacon` |
|---|---|---|
| Placeholder (unset variable) | 0 | absent |
| Token injected | 1 | `{"token":"deadbeefcafe1234"}` |

Conformance sweep: 0 blocking. One pre-existing advisory (`interview-answer-stale` on the `grow_with_claudinite` pack entry) is unrelated to this change and left alone.

## To turn it on

Create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics → "Add a site"), then add its token as the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repo variable (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables). It works on GitHub Pages as-is — no hosting or DNS move needed. Until then the site deploys exactly as it does today, with analytics off.

Closes #35

Both sites now carry analytics, following EdFringeNow's pattern exactly:

- **MissingBulbWebsite — [PR #20](https://github.com/missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite/pull/20)** (closes #19)
- **ClaudiniteWebsite — [PR #36](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/pull/36)** (closes #35)

The pattern I copied from EdFringeNow: a `analytics.js` loader holding a placeholder token that returns immediately while the placeholder is in place, with the Pages deploy substituting the real token from a `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repo **variable** (public, since the beacon token ships in the client — a variable, not a secret). Nothing breaks when the variable is unset; the sites deploy exactly as they do today with analytics simply off.

I verified both states in headless Chromium against the real files, using the same `sed` line the workflows run: placeholder → **0** beacon requests; injected token → **1** request with the correct `data-cf-beacon` payload. Both repos' conformance sweeps pass.

Two judgment calls worth flagging:

- **I included a privacy page in each.** EdFringeNow's approach isn't just the loader — it ships a privacy disclosure naming Cloudflare and explaining the cookieless, no-consent-banner rationale. Turning on data collection without the matching disclosure would leave each site making a promise it no longer keeps, so the page ships in the same commit as the behaviour. Each is styled with its own site's tokens and linked from the footer.
- **ClaudiniteWebsite's "no third-party assets" claim:** that site advertises no webfonts, frameworks, or external assets. The default build preserves that exactly — the beacon only ever loads once you deliberately set the token. I noted this in the PR.

**To switch either on:** create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics → "Add a site") and add its token as the `CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` repo variable under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables. Works on GitHub Pages as-is, no DNS move.

> ⚠️ **Still open:** review and merge PR #20 and PR #36 (say "LGTM" and I'll land them), then add the Cloudflare token variable in each repo to actually start collecting. Note that MissingBulbWebsite's `main` currently has no open work besides #20.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc. - **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control. - **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.) - **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of. - **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked. # Claudinite — active-pack guidance The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand. # Working discipline The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project. Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. 1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule. 2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes. 3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it. The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for. Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided. When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs. When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out. Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere. Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet. When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change. An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. # The task lifecycle The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill. For every new task: 1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work. 2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`). 3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done. --- # HTML Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. --- # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape, growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc (`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`). - **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. - **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header. - **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header doesn't move. - **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may build on. - **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current. - **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open questions in both directions. - **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR. - **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones. - **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The repo's own scheduler runs the pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md), [single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md), [single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)). The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.** - **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name. - **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites **its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body. --- # session-tooling — rules ## Never use WebFetch to obtain content you must have `WebFetch` fails two different ways in this environment, and both were paid for in one session: - **It summarizes.** Asked for "the complete verbatim content" of a raw `githubusercontent.com` file, it returned a prose description of the document instead. The file had to be re-fetched with `curl -sSL -o /f.md ` and read from disk — the correct move the first time. - **It 403s.** Four consecutive fetches of ordinary publisher pages (`gartner.com`, `fortunebusinessinsights.com`, `marketdataforecast.com`, `squarerootseo.com`) all returned `403 Forbidden`, so a research pass ended up attributing figures to search snippets instead of verifying them at source. When a page 403s, do **not** retry it or try a sibling URL — take the `WebSearch` snippet, attribute it to the publisher rather than asserting it, and flag it for re-verification. `WebSearch` itself works fine and is the right first reach. **`codeload.github.com` is blocked here too** — `curl … | tar -xz` of a repo tarball returns 403. Use `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com//`, which works through the proxy and yields the same tree. ## A ToolSearch that finds nothing does not mean the tool is absent Deferred tools are matched by keyword, and the keywords are not the tool's own vocabulary. A session searched `"create trigger routine scheduled task automation"`, got back `TaskCreate`/`CronCreate`/etc., concluded there was no trigger API in the session, and told the owner to create a scheduled routine by hand — while `create_trigger` was in its tool list the whole time. The owner's reply was "Why didn't you create the routine? You should have." Before telling the owner a step is theirs because the capability is missing: search the **literal name** (`select:create_trigger`), and try the tool. A negative keyword search is evidence about the query, not about the environment — and handing the owner work the session could have done is the expensive half of the mistake. --- # Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing) Each pack states what it owns and what it does not.
